content: Colombian Sign Language is a language utilized by an estimated 250,000 deaf individuals in Colombia. In 1992, approximately 50,000 deaf people in Bogotá were reported to use this language. The development of Colombian Sign Language has been influenced by both Spanish Sign Language and American Sign Language. Additionally, similarities with the sign language used in El Salvador have been observed. In Bogotá, there are two schools dedicated to teaching sign language, with the first one established in 1929. Medellín also has two such schools, and Cali has one. Across the country, three different institutions actively support the promotion and learning of Colombian Sign Language. The National Committee for Sign Language plays a significant role in advancing research in this field, distributing resources such as the manual alphabet for spelling and the Grammar Dictionary, and supporting the organization of sign language teacher training programs. Furthermore, the national telecommunications center, TELECOM, provides a CD-ROM software designed for self-learning of the language. There is a growing interest among hearing individuals in learning Colombian Sign Language. Some schools have incorporated the use of sign language into their classrooms. Interpreters are made available at important public events and for college students to ensure accessibility. Colombian Sign Language software is available through the Lengua de Señas Colombianas program, developed by the Research Division of ITEC TELECOM Colombia.
